newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sentrachem restructuring may be reviewed.
newsitem.headline: Sentrachem restructuring may be reviewed.

text.p: South African chemicals firm Sentrachem Ltd said on Monday that elements of a huge restructuring would come under review if an offer for the firm by U.S. group Dow Chemical is successful.

Sentrachem embarked on the massive programme last month as it posted a first half pre-tax loss of 257 million rand ($55.3 million) following one-off charges of 261 million rand due to forward cover contracts and restructuring costs at its Sanachem unit.

Sentrachem managing director John Job said elements of the programme, involving possible disposals and a study into listing a speciality chemicals firm based around its Hampshire Chemicals unit in London or New York, would now be reviewed.
"A lot of it (the restructuring programme) has to be looked at again," he told Reuters.

But Job added that many of the cost-cutting elements of the restructuring would still go ahead. They included moves such as a merger of its NCP and Karbochem units and plans to cut costs by 300-350 million rand at its Sanachem unit.

Dow, the world's fifth biggest chemicals firm with annual sales of more than $20 billion, has already sealed an agreement from Sankorp Ltd, which holds 38.74 percent of Sentrachem, to accept and recommend its 10.50 rand a share offer.
The bid values Sentrachem at 2.074 billion rand.

Job said it was too early to say how a successful bid -- which seems highly likely -- would affect other parts of the group in terms of job losses, disposals not planned in the restructuring and any rebranding.
"No disposals or job losses have been discussed at this time. We are just discussing the purchase procedure," he said.

Dow's move for the firm came very swiftly with the first offical approach being made to Sentrachem just last Thursday. "The offer was made on Thursday, but you don't move that quickly without doing your homework," Job said.
Job said Sentrachem would benefit from the takeover by getting access to one of the world's leading chemicals companies and that the fit between the two was highly complementary.
The news first broke when Sentrachem's shares were suspended earlier on Monday by the Johannesburg Stock Exchange pending an announcement.
The share closed on Friday at 792 cents and dealers said the stock would rapidly rise to its 10.50 price tag when trading in the shares resumes.

The market welcomed the news, saying it was a good price and would help make up for the firm's recent poor results. "It is about time Sentrachem came out with some good news," said Peer Ieul, managing director at UAL Securities.
A JSE spokeswoman said it had not yet been decided when the firm's shares would restart trading.
